title: Skin and eye exposure
audience: Car detailers and their supervisors who plan shifts that involve washing, degreasing, drying and product application.
learningOutcomes: Identify the repeated wet-work and splash exposures in a detailing shift.
Select chemical-resistant gloves using the SDS and use them correctly.
Plan task rotation and drying breaks to reduce wet-work exposure, and refer persistent symptoms.

instruction.heading: Wet work and what it does to skin
instruction.body: Detailing involves repeated wet work. Safe Work Australia defines wet work in three ways: having body parts in liquids, or wearing waterproof gloves or other waterproof PPE, for more than two hours a shift; handling wet items for more than two hours; or washing hands more than 20 times a shift. A two-bucket wash, a decontamination session and drying can meet several of these tests in a single day. The most common work-related contact dermatitis is irritant contact dermatitis, which develops from repeated or long exposure that damages the skin's protective barrier. Detergent, degreaser and solvent can all do this, and so can wet hands kept inside gloves. Early signs include dry, red, painful or itchy skin, cracking, peeling, and a stinging or burning feeling. The hands are affected most often, but the condition can spread to the arms and face and can take months to heal. Allergic contact dermatitis is different. It is an allergic reaction, can appear up to 72 hours after exposure, and is likely to last once it develops. A worker who reports a rash or ongoing skin change should not be told to keep working through it.

instruction.heading: Splashes to the eyes and face
instruction.body: Eye exposure happens when spraying and rinsing, when product or water bounces back from a surface, or when a hose is moved. Degreasers are often misted onto the lower body first and worked up the vehicle, which can throw droplets towards face height. Splashes also happen when a worker bends to clean a wheel arch, or wrings a cloth over a bucket. Eye protection is needed whenever a splash is possible, and it has to fit and be worn for the whole task. PPE is the last line of defence. The Safe Work Australia guidance on PPE says it is one of the least effective controls and should be considered only after higher-level measures, such as removing or substituting the hazard. In a detailing business, the higher-level measures are choosing a less hazardous product, diluting to the label, spraying low and away from the face, and using a bucket and wringing method that limits splashes. PPE is worn in addition to those controls, not instead of them. The business must provide the PPE the worker needs, train workers to use, clean and store it, and make sure it fits and protects the wearer.

instruction.heading: Gloves: choosing and using them
instruction.body: Choose gloves from the SDS. Section 8 of an SDS covers exposure controls and personal protection, and it names the glove material suited to the product. A thin disposable glove is useful for some light tasks, but it is not a substitute for a chemical-resistant glove when handling a concentrate. Replace gloves that are torn, swollen or contaminated on the inside. Put on clean, dry hands, and remove gloves by peeling them inside out so the outside does not touch bare skin. Wash and dry hands after removal. Gloves trap sweat, which makes wet work worse, so change gloves at breaks and do not reuse disposable ones. Where a worker is sensitive to latex, choose a glove material that does not contain latex. Where a worker has an existing skin condition, discuss the glove choice and the task rotation with the worker and their medical adviser before the shift.

instruction.heading: Task rotation, drying breaks and escalation
instruction.body: Plan the shift so wet work is spread out. Pair the wash with dry tasks such as interior vacuuming, checklists and applying products that do not need wet hands, and schedule drying breaks between wet tasks. Write the plan on the shift sheet, including the break times. If a worker reports persistent skin symptoms, stop the task that causes them, take the worker off wet tasks, and refer them for medical or occupational advice. Record the symptom report, the task that came before it, the action taken and the advice received, with the worker's agreement to the record. Review the plan if the symptoms return. Use the business's own rule for when to seek advice, and do not wait for symptoms to become severe.

procedure: Check each product's SDS for the glove and eye protection named in its PPE section.
Identify the wet-work and splash points in the shift plan before the first wash.
Select and check gloves for tears before each task.
Use eye protection whenever spraying, rinsing or wringing near the face.
Rotate wet and dry tasks and schedule drying breaks, and record the plan.
Remove gloves carefully, wash and dry hands at breaks, and replace torn or contaminated gloves.
Report persistent skin or eye symptoms, stop the causing task, and refer the worker.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person team is booked for three cars in one day: a two-bucket wash, a clay session and a full interior clean.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you plan the shift to limit wet work and splash exposure?
workedExamples.reasoning: List every wet step and estimate how long each worker's hands are in water or wet gloves. Place the interior clean and the checklists between the wet tasks, and schedule a drying break after the wash and another after the clay. Give the worker who is spraying degreaser eye protection, and keep the spray low and away from the face. Record the plan on the shift sheet before work starts.

workedExamples.situation: A worker has cracked, sore hands after a week of degreasing three cars a day. The skin is red and stings under the gloves.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do on the day the worker reports this?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the degreasing task for that worker. Check the gloves against the SDS and replace any that are damaged or the wrong material. Arrange medical or occupational advice, and do not require the worker to continue wet work while waiting. Share the wet tasks across the team and add dry tasks to the worker's day. Record the report and the action taken, with the worker's agreement to the record, and review the plan when the worker returns.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves of the material the SDS names, with a spare pair.
Eye protection that fits the worker, including over prescription glasses where needed.
Drying towels and a dry, clean area for breaks.
Skin care product approved by the business for use after wet work. It is not a detailing product.
Shift plan sheet with rotation and break times.

commonErrors.error: Waiting for skin damage before changing the plan.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the wet work at the start of the shift and review it at the first symptom report.

commonErrors.error: Using household or general cleaning gloves for a concentrate.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose the glove material named in the SDS.

commonErrors.error: Keeping damp gloves on through a break.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove gloves, dry the hands and change gloves at each break.
Spray low, work from the bottom up, and wear eye protection.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Employers must provide the PPE that workers need, train workers in its use, cleaning and storage, and make sure it fits and protects the wearer (Safe Work Australia PPE guidance). PPE is among the least effective controls and comes after higher-level measures.

The Safe Work Australia contact dermatitis overview names wet work and irritant exposure as risk factors and directs workplace questions to the state or territory WHS authority. The wet-work definition in this lesson is the one the overview gives. Occupational health advice is available through the worker's medical provider.

qualityStandard: Shift plan shows every wet task and each drying break, and is agreed before work starts.
Gloves and eye protection match the SDS for each product in use and are checked before each task.
A worker with persistent symptoms is removed from the causing task and referred, and the report is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Shift plan with rotation and break times.
SDS reference for the gloves and eye protection for each product used.
Symptom report, task, action and referral record, with the worker's agreement to the record.
summary: Count the wet work in every shift before the shift starts.
Use the glove and eye protection named in the SDS, and treat PPE as the last control.
Act on the first report of persistent skin or eye symptoms.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is wet work, as Safe Work Australia defines it?
options: Using a dry microfibre cloth for a short inspection of the paint surface on the car
Carrying a dry checklist between cars during the morning inspection round today
Keeping hands in liquid or waterproof gloves for more than two hours a shift
Vacuuming a carpet with a dry brush in the car for a short time at the start

knowledgeChecks.question: How do you choose chemical-resistant gloves for a product?
options: Use the glove material named in the SDS for that product
Choose the cheapest disposable glove on the shelf for the job
Use any glove that fits over the wrist for the job today
Use household gloves for all products used on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has had red, cracked hands for a week. What is the correct response?
options: Ask the worker to keep going until the end of the job, since the hands will settle
Apply a heavy dressing to the hands and continue with the work the same day
Stop the causing task, check the gloves and refer the worker for advice
Wait a month to see whether it clears by itself without any action
